books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Henry David Thoreau, “Resistance to Civil Government,” 1849

stimulus.source_note: Henry David Thoreau, “Resistance to Civil Government,” published May 1849 in Aesthetic Papers. Public domain.
stimulus.text:
How does it become a man to behave toward this American government to-day? I answer, that he cannot without disgrace be associated with it. I cannot for an instant recognize that political organization as my government which is the slave's government also.

. . .

But when the friction comes to have its machine, and oppression and robbery are organized, I say, let us not have such a machine any longer. In other words, when a sixth of the population of a nation which has undertaken to be the refuge of liberty are slaves, and a whole country is unjustly overrun and conquered by a foreign army, and subjected to military law, I think that it is not too soon for honest men to rebel and revolutionize.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Compared with Lincoln's Spot Resolutions of 1847, Thoreau's protest differs most in which of the following ways?

options.text: Lincoln supported the war while Thoreau opposed it.
options.misconception: Lincoln also opposed the war; he challenged Polk's justification for it in Congress.

options.text: Thoreau wanted the United States to annex all of Mexico, while Lincoln did not.
options.misconception: Thoreau wanted no conquest at all; annexing all of Mexico was the demand of expansionists, not of Thoreau.

options.text: Lincoln challenged the war inside Congress, while Thoreau refused the government outside it.
Thoreau defended slavery while Lincoln attacked it.
options.misconception: Thoreau calls the government “the slave's government” as a condemnation, not a defense.

rationales.A: Lincoln opposed the war too; his resolutions demanded proof that Mexico had invaded American soil.
rationales.B: Thoreau opposed the war and its conquests; taking all of Mexico was an expansionist demand, not his.
rationales.C: Lincoln worked through resolutions in the House; Thoreau refused his tax and accepted jail, acting as a private citizen.
rationales.D: Thoreau condemns the government for upholding slavery; he does not defend the institution.
rationales.general:
1. Set the two men side by side. Lincoln was a congressman; Thoreau was a writer in Massachusetts.
2. Compare their tools. Lincoln filed resolutions and demanded facts; Thoreau refused a tax and went to jail.
3. See the shared ground and the split. Both opposed the war, but one fought it in Congress and the other by withdrawing himself.
Remember: opposition to a war can wear two shapes — a question asked in the Capitol, and a tax refused at home.
